name: 02-first-look-esp32
description: The same tree on real hardware: what a device adds that a computer cannot, from LED pins to a microphone.

steps.title: Your device
steps.caption: Your device. Every module, top to bottom.
The same tree as on a computer, card for card. What changes is what is behind it: this one has pins, a radio and a microphone.
Layouts: where your lights physically are.
Grid: width, height and depth. This one is sixty four by sixty four, which is four thousand and ninety six lights on a device that costs a few euros.
Effects: what they show, stacked in layers.
Layer: one effect and its modifiers, blended onto the ones below. The one running here is Pulse, which is what you have been watching.
Drivers: how the finished frame reaches the lights. The palette lives here too, which is where every effect takes its colors from.
An output driver is added per device rather than built in, so here is one: the R M T driver, which clocks a strip from a single pin.
A pin, a light count, and the preset that says which channel does what. That is the whole contract between a frame and a wire.
A driver does not have to drive a wire at all. This one sends the finished frame over the network instead.
Art Net, s A C N or DDP, to anything that listens: the same frame the strip gets, addressed to another device.
System: the device itself, its chip, its uptime, how fast it renders.
Tasks: what runs each frame, and what each costs in microseconds.
I2cScan: on real hardware it finds the chips actually wired to the bus.
Pins: which pin every module has claimed, so two never fight over one.
File Manager: this is the device's own flash, so a backup here is worth taking.
Network: the WiFi it joined, and the other devices it can see.
Mqtt: a broker, so the device answers to a home automation system on its own.
Devices: now that this one is on the network, it finds the others and they find it.
Services: the inputs, and on a device they read real pins.
Audio: this device has a microphone, so it is listening to the room.
Firmware: it finds the next release and installs it over the air. This one is an S3.
Behind it sits MoonBase, a second boot image that ships on the four megabyte devices. It is what brings a classic ESP32 back when an update goes wrong.
MoonCloud: what everyone else is running, which this device can now join.
Stats: what this device would share, and the totals it gets back.
Consent is off until someone turns it on. On it goes, and this device starts reporting into those totals.
Talk: ask a question from the device itself, without leaving the page.
And Talk, so a question asked here reaches everyone running the same firmware.
